explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), opens with “To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:” (Ecclesiastes 3:1). Everything and every purpose, so nothing gets left out. That's a guest list with no one standing outside.

That's right, baker. The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), says “To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:” (Ecclesiastes 3:1). He doesn't pick out a few favorite parts of life. Even a batch of cookies has its time in the oven.

explanations.answer: A time to be born and a time to die
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Verse 2 says “a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot,” (Ecclesiastes 3:2). The first day and the last day of a life sit side by side in one line. He could have started small, but he went straight to the big stuff.

explanations.answer: A time to wake and a time to sleep
explanations.explanation: Waking and sleeping do feel like a natural pair, friend. But they aren't in his list. He opens with “a time to be born and a time to die,” (Ecclesiastes 3:2). That's the very start and the very end of a life.

explanations.answer: A time to come and a time to go
explanations.explanation: Come and go sounds like it could fit, and I see why you picked it. But his words are born and die. Ecclesiastes 3:2 puts a time to be born right beside a time to die. Those are the first and last moments of a life, so he starts with the biggest ones.

You got it, baker. Born goes with die, plant goes with uproot, and break down goes with build (Ecclesiastes 3:2-3). Every time in his list has its opposite waiting right beside it. Pairs all the way down.

Reward is a fun guess, friend, but nothing in these verses hands out prizes. Born is paired with die, plant with uproot, and break down with build (Ecclesiastes 3:2-3). Each time sits next to its opposite. It's a list of matching pairs, not a list of rewards.

Reasons would be handy, I'll admit. But in these verses the Teacher doesn't attach a reason to any of them. He pairs born with die, plant with uproot, and break down with build (Ecclesiastes 3:2-3). What each one gets paired with is its opposite.

That's it, baker. The verse says “a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance,” (Ecclesiastes 3:4). Tears sit on one side and laughter on the other, and mourning sits right beside dancing. I think that's what makes this list feel so honest about life.

Work and rest are real parts of life, friend, but they aren't in this line. Here the Teacher pairs weeping with laughing and mourning with dancing (Ecclesiastes 3:4). Those are sad times matched with glad ones. Work comes up later in the passage.

Ages of life aren't what this line is about, friend. The Teacher pairs “a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance,” (Ecclesiastes 3:4). That's sorrow matched with joy. Nothing in it mentions how old anybody is.
True, baker. Verse 5 says “a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing,” (Ecclesiastes 3:5). So it names the hug and also the holding back. Even this part of the list comes in a pair.

Careful, friend, because the text does say it. Verse 5 reads “a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing,” (Ecclesiastes 3:5). The holding back is right there next to the hug. The Teacher keeps his pairs tidy.

Right, baker. Verse 6 says “a time to keep and a time to discard,” (Ecclesiastes 3:6). Keeping gets its season and so does letting go. Anybody who has ever cleaned out a closet knows both of those times are real.

Save is a close cousin of keep, friend, and that's the trouble. It sits on the same side instead of the opposite one. The Teacher says “a time to keep and a time to discard,” (Ecclesiastes 3:6). His pattern pairs each time with its opposite, so discard it is.

Sharing is a kind thing to do, friend, but it isn't in this line. The verse says “a time to keep and a time to discard,” (Ecclesiastes 3:6). Following his pattern, keep gets matched with its opposite. That makes it discard.

That's right, baker. The verse says “a time to be silent and a time to speak.” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). Silence and speech both get their seasons. I think the hard part is knowing which one the moment is asking for.

Rest is a nice thought, friend, but it isn't the word he uses. The Teacher says “a time to be silent and a time to speak.” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). Silent is paired with speak, its opposite. Rest isn't in this pair.

Listening does go hand in hand with being quiet, I'll give you that. But the verse says “a time to be silent and a time to speak.” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). The opposite of silent in his pattern is speak. That's the word he picked.

You got it, baker. The last line of his list says “a time for war and a time for peace.” (Ecclesiastes 3:8). The list closes with the same kind of pair it has used the whole way through. War gets matched with its opposite, peace.

Rest sounds lovely after a war, friend, but it's not the word in the verse. The Teacher says “a time for war and a time for peace.” (Ecclesiastes 3:8). Following his pattern, war is matched with its opposite. That's peace.

Victory is what a lot of people would expect to follow war, friend. But the verse doesn't say it. It says “a time for war and a time for peace.” (Ecclesiastes 3:8). His pairs are always opposites, so peace goes with war.

That's the one, baker. The Teacher says, “He has made everything beautiful in its time.” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Everything, and in its time. After all those seasons of weeping and war, that's a gentle thing to hear.

Easy would be nice, wouldn't it, friend? But that's not the word he uses. The Teacher says, “He has made everything beautiful in its time.” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Beautiful is the word, and the verse doesn't say it's easy.

Quick would sure save some trouble, friend. Anyone who has stared at a slow oven knows how that feels. But the verse says, “He has made everything beautiful in its time.” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). The word is beautiful, and it's tied to its time.

Not quite, friend. The verse says people “cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end.” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). It follows right after the line about eternity set in their hearts. So the Teacher says they can't take in all of it, from start to finish.

Right, baker. The Teacher says God “has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end.” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). They can't take in all of it, from start to finish. It's a lot bigger than any of us.

Yes, baker. He says, “I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live,” (Ecclesiastes 3:12). Two simple things, and he says nothing is better. That's the answer I'd been hoping somebody would write down.

Gathering sounds sensible, friend, but it's not what the verse says. He says, “I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live,” (Ecclesiastes 3:12). Rejoicing and doing good are the two things he names. Nothing in that verse is about collecting more.

That one would wear out even a stamper with hardy edges, friend. The verse doesn't say it. The Teacher says, “I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live,” (Ecclesiastes 3:12). What he names is rejoicing and doing good.

That's it, baker. Verse 13 says every man should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his labor, and then, “this is the gift of God.” (Ecclesiastes 3:13). A gift is something handed to you, not something you earn. And it includes the labor part.

A test would make a person nervous at the dinner table, friend. But that's not the word. The verse says, “this is the gift of God.” (Ecclesiastes 3:13). Eating, drinking and satisfaction in labor get called a gift.
A price tag, huh? I once had a 25 cent sticker on me myself, so I know the feeling. But the Teacher doesn't call this a price. He says, “this is the gift of God.” (Ecclesiastes 3:13).

That's right, baker. The Teacher says, “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Seasons come and go in his list, but God's work lasts. It keeps going forever.

I get why that one looked tempting, since the whole list is about time. But the Teacher says the opposite. He says, “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). God's work doesn't fade.

That fits the first half of the passage, friend, where times keep trading places. But verse 14 says something else about God's work. “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). It lasts, and it doesn't change.

True, baker. The verse says, “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Nothing taken, nothing added. My own cookie dough could never promise that, since somebody always sneaks a scoop.

Look again, friend, because it does say that. The Teacher says, “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Taking from it is on the list of things nobody can do. God's work stays just as it is.

explanations.answer: So that people would fear Him
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Verse 14 ends, “God does it so that they should fear Him.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). The Teacher gives that as the reason. It comes right after the part about God's work lasting forever.

explanations.answer: So that people would rest from work
explanations.explanation: Resting sounds nice, friend, but the verse doesn't give that as the reason. It says, “God does it so that they should fear Him.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). That's the reason the Teacher states. Rest isn't part of that line.

explanations.answer: So that kings would rule wisely
explanations.explanation: Kings are not in that verse, friend. The Teacher says, “God does it so that they should fear Him.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). That's the reason he gives. It's about people, not rulers.
True, baker. The last line says, “for God will call to account what has passed.” (Ecclesiastes 3:15). That's how the passage closes. The Teacher says it plainly and moves on.
Check the last verse, friend, because it's right there. The Teacher says, “for God will call to account what has passed.” (Ecclesiastes 3:15). That's how his passage ends. So the answer is true.
